strengths: Clear problem motivation addressing overfitting and spurious features in few-shot WSI classification
Solid theoretical contributions with rigorous approximation guarantee (Theorem 1) using random matrix theory
Elegant plug-and-play design requiring no architectural modifications with 226× fewer parameters than ViLaMIL
Comprehensive experimental validation across 3 datasets, 4-5 MIL architectures, and multiple few-shot settings (k=1-16)
Thorough ablation studies examining components, activation functions, initialization methods, layer positions, and rank sensitivity
Consistent improvements over strong baselines including state-of-the-art methods
Practical applicability with minimal computational overhead suitable for clinical deployment
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (low-rank factorization, frozen random matrices from ELM) without fundamentally new insights
Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 proves approximation capability but doesn't rigorously explain why this improves generalization in few-shot settings beyond establishing a lower bound
High variance in results with unclear statistical significance (e.g., ABMIL/Camelyon16/k=1: 0.594±0.124; TCGA-NSCLC/k=16 marginal improvements)
Hyperparameter rank r fixed at 64 across all layers/datasets acknowledged as suboptimal with no principled selection strategy provided
Unfair comparison with ViLaMIL: methods solve different problems (vision-language fusion vs parameter-efficient linear replacement) with different objectives
Limited evaluation scope: only histopathology domain tested; generalization claims to other domains speculative and unvalidated
Missing comparisons with recent parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, adapters, other low-rank techniques) and few-shot regularization approaches
Dense presentation with 9 tables relegating critical proofs to appendix; unclear which feature extractor used in main Table 1 results

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 datasets, 5 MIL architectures, and k=1-16 shot settings with thorough ablations and sensitivity analyses
Practical and simple method suitable for real applications with 226× parameter reduction vs. ViLaMIL and no architectural changes required
Consistent improvements across multiple MIL frameworks and good experimental rigor with multiple runs and standard deviations reported
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation and methodology
Extensive implementation details and dataset-specific configurations provided for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combines well-known techniques (low-rank factorization, random projections) in straightforward manner without substantial new insights
Theorem 1 is essentially trivial—merely restates that any matrix can be approximated by adding a random matrix plus low-rank correction; lacks fundamental theoretical insight
High variance in results with overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., Camelyon16 k=1) makes statistical significance of improvements unclear; no significance testing performed
Weak justification for design choices: frozen vs. trainable recalibration matrix not compared; fixed rank r=64 despite sensitivity analysis showing r=4 sometimes better
Misleading claims: title 'Beyond Linearity' overstates the contribution; 'drop-in replacement' claim contradicted by model-specific layer modifications (Appendix D.3)
Missing comparisons with other low-rank methods, alternative regularization techniques, and parameter reduction schemes
Dataset-specific performance: strong improvements only on easier tasks (RCC, NSCLC with high baselines) but minimal gains on hardest task (Camelyon16)
Evaluation limited to pathology domain only; claims of broad applicability unsupported
Abrupt ablation design: '- Random' removes entire component catastrophically rather than comparing frozen vs. trainable matrix
Insufficient analysis of core mechanism: no rigorous justification for why low-rank pathway + frozen random matrix specifically prevents spurious feature learning

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing genuine challenges in few-shot WSI classification (annotation scarcity, overfitting, spurious features)
Elegant drop-in design requiring zero architectural modifications to existing MIL models
Solid theoretical justification with universal approximation guarantee (Theorem 1) and comprehensive geometric property preservation proofs

Exceptionally thorough experimental evaluation: multiple shot settings (k=1-16), diverse architectures (ABMIL, CLAM, TransMIL, CATE), three datasets, extensive ablations, and multiple feature extractors
Impressive parameter efficiency with 226× reduction vs ViLaMIL while maintaining/improving performance
Consistent empirical improvements across all settings with particularly strong gains on challenging Camelyon16 dataset (34.6% AUC improvement)
Comprehensive sensitivity analyses on rank parameter, activation functions, initialization schemes, and feature extractors
Good reproducibility with clear implementation details and code release commitment
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines well-established techniques (low-rank factorization, frozen random projections from ELM/random kitchen sinks) without introducing fundamentally new concepts

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 only formally proves linear case; universal approximation for non-linear version invoked but not proved. More critically, approximation guarantee doesn't explain why SR prevents overfitting and spurious features

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: catastrophic performance degradation with -Random (Table 2) is not deeply analyzed; claims about spurious feature prevention lack direct validation beyond metrics
Limited experimental scope: only WSI classification tested despite broad applicability claims; all three datasets are cancer-related; true generalization to other domains not demonstrated

Methodological concerns: fixed rank r=64 across all experiments with no principled selection strategy; r=4 sometimes outperforms r=64 but this phenomenon unexplained; comparison with VLMs unfair as they access text information
Missing comparisons with other few-shot learning baselines (prototypical networks, matching networks) and parameter-reduction techniques beyond VLMs
Incomplete ablations: trained vs frozen recalibration matrix not compared; layer-wise analysis limited to ABMIL; limited exploration of alternative random initializations
Statistical rigor: no significance tests provided; some improvements modest and within standard deviation ranges
Misleading title 'Beyond Linearity' when method fundamentally relies on linear transformations with bottleneck constraints

strengths: Novel geometric perspective framing few-shot overfitting as manifold degradation, with rigorous three-pronged empirical evidence (spectral analysis, t-SNE, tangent space analysis)
Solid theoretical grounding with comprehensive geometric preservation proofs (Appendix D) and universal approximation guarantees (Theorem E.1)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 MIL architectures, 6+ baselines, multiple datasets and shot settings with proper capacity-matched ablations
Plug-and-play design that improves parameter efficiency while maintaining consistent performance improvements across diverse settings
Extensive ablation studies examining component effects, initialization robustness, rank sensitivity, and generalization beyond extreme few-shot regime
Well-presented paper with clear motivation, excellent visualizations (especially Figure 1), and thorough appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Weak causal link between manifold preservation and improved generalization—paper explicitly treats geometric metrics as 'qualitative diagnostics' rather than direct performance predictors, lacking formal justification
Contradictory evidence in Figure 1(d): LRP alone causes significant tangent drift, suggesting the random anchor does most of the work and undermining the task-specific adaptation motivation
Limited architectural novelty—the MR block is essentially a fixed random matrix plus low-rank residual (similar to LoRA), with the innovation being primarily motivational rather than structural
Weak theoretical guarantees: universal approximation theorem requires rank up to min(d₀, d₁), contradicting the low-rank premise; provides worst-case but not typical-case guarantees
Causality of feature manifold properties not established—low effective rank appears specific to CONCH's vision-language pretraining; universality across domains and extractors not validated
High experimental variance (Table 1: ±13.5% on some metrics) and lack of statistical significance testing; some MR variants underperform baselines (e.g., MR-DGRMIL on Camelyon16 k=4)
Fixed rank parameter (r=64) suboptimal across all layers; Figure 3 shows peak performance at r≈32 for simpler models, contradicting post-hoc justification linking r to effective rank of 29.7
Frozen random anchor ignores task/dataset information; no exploration of data-driven alternatives (e.g., PCA) mentioned in Appendix I

strengths: Novel geometric perspective on overfitting in few-shot WSI classification with rigorous manifold analysis (spectral, t-SNE, tangent space)
Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple datasets (Camelyon16, TCGA-NSCLC, TCGA-RCC) and shot settings with extensive ablations
Practical parameter efficiency: achieves better performance with significantly fewer parameters than baselines
Thorough experimental protocols with detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Capacity-matched comparisons effectively isolate geometric contributions from parameter reduction
weaknesses: Loose connection between geometric motivation and practice: authors acknowledge geometric metrics are 'qualitative diagnostics' that cannot reliably predict performance improvements, undermining the core geometric justification
Limited methodological novelty: combining frozen random projection with low-rank residual is straightforward; theoretical results rely on standard Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma without novel extensions
Large experimental variance (±15-25pp) makes many claimed improvements statistically marginal and difficult to distinguish from noise; no formal significance testing provided

Unfair theoretical comparisons: Figure 1(d) compares trained linear layers (which must distort geometry for task fitting) against frozen random matrices, conflating task-specific learning with geometric degradation
Incomplete analysis: no comparison with other geometric regularization methods (spectral normalization, Lipschitz constraints), and limited explanation of failure cases (e.g., DGRMIL results)
Arbitrary hyperparameter selection: rank r=64 appears unmotivated when Figure 3 suggests saturation at r≈32; no principled guidance for practitioners

Questionable claims about geometry preservation: GELU nonlinearity in LRP contradicts preservation claims; insensitivity to initialization (Table 5) suggests randomness may not be crucial for the geometric mechanism
Limited generalization scope: all analysis based on patch-level WSI features; claims about broader applicability to other domains are entirely speculative

strengths: Compelling geometric perspective on manifold degradation with multi-faceted evidence (spectral analysis, t-SNE, tangent space drift)
Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 datasets, multiple shot settings, 5 MIL architectures with extensive ablations
Theoretically grounded approach with universal approximation guarantees and proofs of geometric preservation properties
Practical plug-and-play design achieving parameter efficiency (e.g., 0.10M vs 0.26M for ABMIL) with consistent improvements
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, promised code release
Rigorous ablation studies isolating component contributions (Table 2: removing anchor/LRP severely hurts performance)
weaknesses: Disconnect between geometric motivation and performance: authors acknowledge geometric metrics are 'qualitative diagnostics' that cannot reliably predict dataset-level improvements, undermining the central claim that geometry is the fundamental bottleneck
Modest empirical gains with high variance (e.g., Camelyon16 16-shot MR-CATE ±16.9 AUC; NSCLC capacity-matched shows 78.7 vs 86.5); improvements often smaller than baseline variance
Limited architectural novelty: MR block combines standard components (random projection via Johnson-Lindenstrauss, low-rank factorization similar to LoRA, residual connection)

Incomplete mechanistic isolation: unable to distinguish whether benefits derive from geometry preservation vs. low-rank regularization alone; no ablations with alternative anchor designs (e.g., PCA-based)
Narrow scope: tested only on patch-level foundation models (CONCH, UNI, ResNet50), no experiments outside WSI domain despite generality claims; excluded slide-level models (TITAN)
Statistical rigor gaps: no significance testing, overlapping error bars with baselines in some cases yet presented as improvements, no confidence intervals

Geometric analysis limitations: k=12 nearest neighbor sensitivity unexplored, tangent drift values small (0.2-0.6 range), effective rank alignment (29.7 predicted vs 32 observed) could be coincidental
